item.stem:
The cyanate ion, OCN⁻ (16 valence electrons), has carbon as the central atom. Three candidate Lewis structures are described below. Electronegativity order: O > N > C.

Structure I: O=C=N, with 2 lone pairs on O and 2 lone pairs on N
Structure II: O≡C–N, with 1 lone pair on O and 3 lone pairs on N
Structure III: O–C≡N, with 3 lone pairs on O and 1 lone pair on N

Which claim about the best representation of OCN⁻ is supported by formal-charge reasoning?

choices.choice_text: Structure I, because it has the fewest nonzero formal charges, with only −1 on nitrogen.
choices.rationale: This stops at the first criterion. Structures I and III tie, each with a single −1 charge, and the tiebreak favors negative charge on oxygen, which is more electronegative than nitrogen. Fix: When structures tie on formal charges, check which one puts the negative charge on the more electronegative atom.

choices.choice_text: Structure III, because its only nonzero formal charge is −1 and it sits on oxygen, the most electronegative atom.
choices.rationale: Formal charge = valence − lone-pair electrons − ½ bonding electrons. In III, O = 6 − 6 − 1 = −1, C = 4 − 0 − 4 = 0, N = 5 − 2 − 3 = 0. This ties for the fewest nonzero charges and places the negative charge on the most electronegative atom.

choices.choice_text: Structure II, because its formal charges add up to −1, matching the charge of the ion.
choices.rationale: This treats the total as the test. Every valid structure of OCN⁻ has formal charges summing to −1, and II actually has the largest charges, +1 on O and −2 on N. Fix: Compute each atom's formal charge and compare their sizes and locations, not just the total.

choices.choice_text: No structure is best, because the ion rapidly switches among all three structures and spends equal time in each.
choices.rationale: This is the resonance-as-switching misconception. The real ion is one averaged structure, and nonequivalent structures do not contribute equally, so the one with the best formal charges represents it most closely. Fix: Ask whether the structures are equivalent, and if not, rank them by formal charge.

votes.reason: The question requires justifying a claim using formal-charge calculations and chemical principles. Students must compare charges across the candidate structures, recognize that I and III tie in minimizing nonzero charges, and use electronegativity to favor the negative charge on oxygen in III.

The question requires evaluating particulate-level Lewis representations to support a claim about the most favored structure (Skill 6.C). It is of medium difficulty because it requires applying the standard two-step formal-charge criteria (minimizing nonzero charges and assigning the remaining negative charge to the more electronegative atom) to reach a conclusion.

The question requires calculating formal charges for multiple Lewis structures and then applying the tie-breaking criterion of placing negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom, combining formal-charge rules with electronegativity and multi-step reasoning.

Selecting Structure III requires mathematical justification via formal-charge calculations plus the chemical principle of placing negative charge on the most electronegative atom to justify the best-structure claim, matching 6.D. It is Hard because it combines charge-minimization with electronegativity tie-breaker across multiple atoms and evaluates three competing structures, not single recall.

item.stem: Three equivalent Lewis diagrams can be drawn for NO₃⁻. In each diagram, N is bonded to three O atoms with one double bond and two single bonds; the double bond is placed on a different O atom in each diagram. Which statement about the actual ion is best justified by this model?

choices.choice_text: All three N–O bonds have the same length, intermediate between typical N–O single- and double-bond lengths, because the ion has one resonance hybrid structure.
choices.rationale: The equivalent diagrams contribute to one resonance hybrid rather than representing separate structures. Each N–O bond has the same intermediate bond order, so all three bonds have equal lengths.

choices.choice_text: The ion rapidly switches among the three diagrams, so each N–O bond alternates between single and double bonds.
choices.rationale: The switching-between-forms misconception treats resonance diagrams as structures visited over time. The ion instead has one structure with equivalent N–O bonds. Fix: Interpret equivalent resonance diagrams as contributors to one structure, not successive snapshots.

choices.choice_text: One N–O bond is permanently shorter than the other two because only one of the three diagrams represents the actual ion.
choices.rationale: The single-diagram trap treats one equivalent contributor as the complete structure. No contributor is preferred, and a permanently localized double bond would incorrectly distinguish one N–O bond from the others. Fix: Check whether the diagrams are equivalent before selecting one as the actual structure.

choices.choice_text: All three N–O bonds are double bonds because that arrangement minimizes the formal charges.
choices.rationale: The formal-charge-only trap ignores the octet rule. Three double bonds would place 12 electrons around nitrogen, which cannot exceed an octet as a second-period element. Fix: Count electrons around nitrogen before using formal charges to rank candidate diagrams.

object.defect: Choice A's wording is slightly imprecise: the ion is described by a single resonance hybrid, not by 'one resonance hybrid structure' in the sense of a single Lewis diagram. Its substance (equal bond lengths, intermediate between single and double) is still clearly correct.

flags: defect: Choice A's wording is slightly imprecise: the ion is described by a single resonance hybrid, not by 'one resonance hybrid structure' in the sense of a single Lewis diagram. Its substance (equal bond lengths, intermediate between single and double) is still clearly correct.

object.defect: Choice A is slightly loose: a single resonance hybrid does not by itself justify equal bond lengths. The equality follows because the three contributing structures are equivalent. This imprecision does not make another choice correct. B describes the classic misconception that the ion flips between structures. C contradicts the equivalence of the three diagrams. D is wrong because three N=O double bonds would give nitrogen an expanded octet, which second-period N cannot have.

This imprecision does not make another choice correct. B describes the classic misconception that the ion flips between structures. C contradicts the equivalence of the three diagrams. D is wrong because three N=O double bonds would give nitrogen an expanded octet, which second-period N cannot have.

item.stem: The thiocyanate ion, SCN⁻, has 16 valence electrons and a central carbon atom. Three candidate Lewis structures are listed. Structure I: S=C=N, with 2 lone pairs on S and 2 lone pairs on N. Structure II: S≡C–N, with 1 lone pair on S and 3 lone pairs on N. Structure III: S–C≡N, with 3 lone pairs on S and 1 lone pair on N. Electronegativities increase in the order C < S < N. Which claim about the best Lewis representation of SCN⁻ does formal-charge reasoning support?

choices.choice_text: Structure III, because it has only one nonzero formal charge, −1 on sulfur.
choices.rationale: This stops after the first criterion. Structures I and III tie with a single −1 charge each, and the tiebreak favors the negative charge on nitrogen, which is more electronegative than sulfur. Fix: When structures tie on formal charges, check which places the negative charge on the more electronegative atom.

choices.choice_text: Structure II, because its formal charges sum to −1, equal to the charge of the ion.
choices.rationale: This uses the total as the deciding test. Every valid structure of SCN⁻ has formal charges summing to −1, and Structure II has the largest charges, +1 on S and −2 on N. Fix: Compute each atom's formal charge and compare magnitudes and locations, not just the sum.

choices.choice_text: Structure I, because its only nonzero formal charge is −1, located on nitrogen, the most electronegative atom.
choices.rationale: Formal charge = valence − lone-pair electrons − ½ bonding electrons. In Structure I, S = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0, C = 4 − 0 − 4 = 0, and N = 5 − 4 − 2 = −1. It ties for the fewest nonzero charges and places the negative charge on the most electronegative atom.

choices.choice_text: None of the structures is best, because the ion rapidly flips among all three and spends equal time in each.
choices.rationale: This is the resonance-as-switching misconception. The real ion is a single averaged structure, and nonequivalent structures do not contribute equally, so the one with the best formal charges represents it most closely. Fix: Ask whether the structures are equivalent, and if not, rank them by formal charge.

item.stem:
A student compares three proposed Lewis diagrams for the thiocyanate ion, SCN⁻, in a salt. The ion contains 16 valence electrons, and its atoms have the electronegativity ranking N > S > C.

Diagram 1: S≡C–N; S has one lone pair, and N has three lone pairs.
Diagram 2: S=C=N; S and N each have two lone pairs.
Diagram 3: S–C≡N; S has three lone pairs, and N has one lone pair.

Carbon has no lone pairs in any diagram. Using the octet rule and formal-charge criteria, which conclusion about the preferred diagram is best justified?

choices.choice_text: Diagram 2 is preferred because it minimizes nonzero formal charges and places the negative formal charge on nitrogen.
choices.rationale: Formal charge equals valence electrons minus lone-pair electrons minus half the bonding electrons. In Diagram 2, S = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0, C = 4 − 0 − 4 = 0, and N = 5 − 4 − 2 = −1. Diagrams 2 and 3 tie in charge minimization, but nitrogen is more electronegative.

choices.choice_text: Diagram 3 is preferred because sulfur carries −1 and every other atom has zero formal charge.
choices.rationale: This is the stopping-after-charge-minimization error. Diagram 2 also has only one −1 formal charge, so the tie is resolved by placing that charge on the more electronegative nitrogen. Fix: After comparing charge magnitudes, compare the electronegativities of atoms carrying negative formal charges.

choices.choice_text: Diagram 1 is preferred because its formal charges sum to the ion’s overall charge of −1.
choices.rationale: This is the total-charge-only error: matching the ion’s charge does not distinguish these diagrams. Diagram 1 assigns +1 to sulfur and −2 to nitrogen, producing greater charge separation than either alternative. Fix: Calculate individual formal charges before comparing their magnitudes and locations.

choices.choice_text: All three diagrams are equally preferred because SCN⁻ alternates among them, spending equal time in each arrangement.
choices.rationale: This is the resonance-as-switching misconception. SCN⁻ has one resonance hybrid rather than alternating structures, and these nonequivalent diagrams do not contribute equally. Fix: Check whether the diagrams are equivalent before ranking their contributions using formal charges.

object.defect: Diagrams 2 and 3 both have only one nonzero formal charge. Diagram 2 is preferred only because it puts the −1 charge on nitrogen, the more electronegative atom, so A's wording 'minimizes' really means 'ties for the minimum'. Experimentally, Diagram 3 also contributes substantially to the real resonance hybrid.

Diagram 2 is preferred only because it puts the −1 charge on nitrogen, the more electronegative atom, so A's wording 'minimizes' really means 'ties for the minimum'. Experimentally, Diagram 3 also contributes substantially to the real resonance hybrid.

object.defect: Minor wording issue: Diagrams 2 and 3 tie on the number of nonzero formal charges, so A's 'minimizes' clause does not distinguish them; the electronegativity tiebreaker does. Real SCN⁻ is a resonance hybrid with a substantial S–C≡N contribution, but under the stated formal-charge criteria A is the intended answer.
